n: The story widens to international politics. Four kings from Mesopotamia and beyond form an alliance. Their identities in history are uncertain, but the names fit the region and era.

f.g: Babylonia (compare 10:10; 11:2).
A kingdom in southwestern Iran.
Hebrew goyim, perhaps a coalition of peoples.

n: These eastern kings attack five city-kings near the Dead Sea, including the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah.
The five kings gather in the valley of Siddim, an area later covered by or bordering the Dead Sea, called here the “salt sea.”

f.g: The Dead Sea, so salty that almost nothing can live in it.

n: The five cities had been subject to Chedorlaomer for twelve years and then rebelled, refusing to pay tribute.

f.g: Paid tribute as subject states.

n: Chedorlaomer’s coalition sweeps down the east side of the Jordan, defeating several peoples remembered as giants or ancient inhabitants.

f.g: An ancient people remembered as giants (Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 20-21).
Another early people of the region east of the Dead Sea (Deuteronomy 2:10).

n: They push on into the mountains of Seir (later Edom) as far as the edge of the wilderness.

f.g: Early inhabitants of Seir, later displaced by Esau’s descendants (Deuteronomy 2:12).
Probably near Elath on the Gulf of Aqaba.

n: Turning back north, they strike Kadesh and the lands of the Amalekites and Amorites. The campaign forms a great loop around the Dead Sea region.

f.g: An oasis in the northern Sinai; Israel later camps there (Numbers 20:1).
“Spring of judgment.”

n: The five rebel kings come out to fight the invaders in the valley of Siddim.

f.g: Engaged in battle.

n: Four kings against five—the larger number loses, showing how powerful the eastern alliance was.

f.g: A neat summary of the conflict.

n: The valley is full of tar pits. The fleeing kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fall into them or hide there; the rest escape to the hills.

f.g: Bitumen or tar pits—natural asphalt deposits common around the Dead Sea.

n: The invaders plunder Sodom and Gomorrah of goods and food supplies.

f.g: Food and provisions.

n: Lot, who now lives in Sodom itself, is captured with his possessions. His choice to live near and then in Sodom has put him in danger.
A survivor brings the news to “Abram the Hebrew,” who is living among friendly Amorite allies near Hebron. This is the first time the word “Hebrew” appears in the Bible.

f.g: First use of “Hebrew,” perhaps from Eber (10:21) or meaning “one from across” the river.
Allied by treaty.

n: Abram immediately rescues his nephew, gathering 318 trained men from his own household and chasing the invaders far to the north.

f.g: Here “brother” means close relative—Lot is his nephew.
The northern town later named Dan (Judges 18:29); the narrator uses the familiar later name.

n: Abram divides his forces and attacks by night, a clever strategy that routs the larger army and pursues them past Damascus.

f.g: A place north of Damascus; location uncertain.
North of (when facing east).

n: Abram recovers everything—Lot, his goods, the women, and the other captives. Abram blesses others, just as God promised he would.

f.g: Brought back; restored.

n: The king of Sodom comes out to meet the victorious Abram in the King’s Valley, likely near Jerusalem.

f.g: The King’s Valley, probably near Jerusalem (compare 2 Samuel 18:18).

n: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, brings bread and wine. Latter-day scripture greatly honors him as a great high priest, after whom the higher priesthood is named.

f.g: Means “king of righteousness.”
Means “peace”; traditionally identified with Jerusalem (Psalms 76:2).
Many see a foreshadowing of the sacrament. JST Genesis 14:25-40 greatly expands Melchizedek’s story.

n: Melchizedek blesses Abram in the name of God, owner of heaven and earth. Doctrine and Covenants teaches that Abraham received the priesthood from Melchizedek.

f.g: Creator or owner.

n: Melchizedek praises God for the victory, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything. This is the first mention of tithing in the Bible.

f.g: A tenth.

n: The king of Sodom offers Abram the captured goods if he will return the people. His offer contrasts sharply with Melchizedek’s gift.

f.g: He wants his subjects back; he offers Abram the plunder.

n: Abram says he has sworn an oath to the Most High God, using the same title Melchizedek used. He identifies the LORD with Melchizedek’s God.

f.w: I have lift up mine hand
f.g: Raising the hand was a gesture of taking an oath.

n: Abram refuses even a thread or sandal strap from Sodom. He wants no one but God to get credit for his prosperity.

f.g: A sandal strap.

f.w: lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich

n: Abram asks only for what his men ate and for his allies’ fair share. He holds himself to a high standard but is fair to others.
